title: The eHALK: Comparing Spatial and Environmental Schemes of Data Borrowing for Age Assignment
content:
ABSTRACT

Fish age-length data are crucial to our understanding of many important processes in fish biology, including growth, mortality, recruitment, and year-class strength. The hierarchical age-length key (HALK) is a recently proposed approach that borrows age-length data along a nested hierarchy of incrementally broader levels, allowing for the estimation of fish ages in systems where age-length data are either sparse or unavailable. Initially developed to adopt spatiotemporal hierarchies, we here propose and test an alternative implementation of the HALK utilizing environmental similarity in place of spatiotemporal proximity. Using length and age-length records for six common freshwater sport fish species from the Upper Midwest, we generated a hierarchical spatial scheme composed of nested, progressively broader hydrologic unit code (HUC) watersheds. We then compared its performance to several similarly structured hierarchical environmental schemes, composed of nested, progressively broader groups of environmentally similar lakes, constructed using various hydrologic, climatic, anthropogenic, and land cover inputs. We found that the performances of environmental models varied among species, but that environmental schemes of data borrowing consistently provided more accurate age estimates than spatial schemes, even when models were constructed based on simple combinations of factors. Our findings suggest that even simple environmental information (e.g., mean catchment temperature, nitrogenous fertilizer application) is a viable and superior alternative to spatial proximity in data borrowing frameworks for age-length models, facilitating improved accuracy of fisheries assessments in data-limited systems. The magnitude and nature of this improvement further varied among species, suggesting that some species-specific ecological traits may modulate the environmental drivers most relevant to growth.
